A Common High Court functioned at Vijayawada.
Andhra Pradesh and Telangana shared a Common High Court at Hyderabad.

Justice Lisa Gill became the first Chief Justice when the court was established in 1954.

Citizenship of India and ten years as a Member of Parliament
Citizenship of India and five years’ experience as an advocate of any court
Citizenship of India and ten years in judicial office or ten years as an advocate of a High Court or High Courts in succession

Chief Justice of India and Governor of the State
Chief Justice of India and Chief Justice of every High Court in India

o: Decided solely by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister
Effected by a simple majority in the concerned Legislative Assembly
Identical to that of a Supreme Court judge and requires an address by both Houses on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Decided by the Chief Justice of India without parliamentary involvement

It is made by Parliament through an ordinary law.
It is made by the Governor after consulting the State Cabinet.

o: Any public-spirited citizen may approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so
A petition can be filed only after approval by Parliament
Only a government officer may file a petition
Only the directly injured person may approach the court

sec: High Courts in India - total number, newest, common High Courts, benches  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding High Court benches:
1. The Bombay High Court has benches at Nagpur, Panaji and Aurangabad.
2. The Calcutta High Court has a circuit bench at Port Blair.
3. The seat of the common High Court for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh is permanently located only at Srinagar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The common High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has its seat at Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Find the false statement by checking the seasonal-seat qualification.
sec: High Courts in India - total number, newest, common High Courts, benches  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following statements regarding the older High Courts in India is correct?
o: Calcutta High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Madras High Court was established in 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Allahabad High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court in India.
Bombay High Court was established in 1862 and is the only oldest High Court in India.
x: Calcutta High Court was established on 2 July 1862 and is the oldest High Court. Madras, Bombay and Allahabad are also among the four oldest High Courts; Madras was also established in 1862.
tq: Separate the oldest institution from the other High Courts established in the same year.
sec: High Courts in India - total number, newest, common High Courts, benches  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The power to establish a common High Court for two or more States, or for States and a Union Territory, is provided under:
x: Article 231 empowers Parliament by law to establish a common High Court for two or more States or for States and a Union Territory.
tq: Match the constitutional Article with the specific institutional power.
sec: Common and new High Courts, UTs - who establishes them, Article 241, UT amendment  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
With reference to High Courts for Union Territories, consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 241, Parliament may constitute a High Court for a Union Territory.
2. Parliament may declare any court in a Union Territory to be a High Court.
3. The President alone may constitute a High Court for a Union Territory without a law made by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 241 authorises Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare a court there to be a High Court. The President alone does not possess this power without parliamentary law.
tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ test to distinguish Parliament’s power from presidential action.
sec: Common and new High Courts, UTs - who establishes them, Article 241, UT amendment  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: A new High Court established under a law made by Parliament comes into being through:
o: A resolution of the concerned State Legislative Assembly
An order of the Chief Justice of India
A notification issued by the Governor alone
A notification issued by the President
x: A new High Court is created under a law made by Parliament and brought into being through a Presidential notification. The Andhra Pradesh High Court was notified by the President under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act.
tq: Distinguish the law-making authority from the authority bringing the institution into effect.
sec: Common and new High Courts, UTs - who establishes them, Article 241, UT amendment  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 13
B. Article 32
C. Article 137
D. Article 226

List-II (Subject)
1. Review of its own judgments by the Supreme Court
2. High Court writ jurisdiction
3. Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights to be void
4. Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for restoration of Fundamental Rights

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Article 13 concerns laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; Article 32 provides Supreme Court writs; Article 137 permits Supreme Court review; and Article 226 concerns High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes.
tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pairs and test the remaining combinations.
sec: Article → subject match  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Article 139A, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, deals with the power of the Supreme Court to:
o: issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
x: Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer certain cases to itself. It was inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
tq: Link the Article number with the distinctive procedural power it confers.
sec: Article → subject match  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
When a government seeks to overcome the effect of a judicial judgment, which of the following may constitutionally be adopted, subject to the Basic Structure limitation?
1. A constitutional amendment altering the legal basis of the decision
2. A valid ordinary or validating law removing the basis of the judgment
3. A simple executive order declaring the judgment inoperative
4. A review petition under Article 137

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: A constitutional amendment, a valid law removing the basis of the judgment, and a review petition under Article 137 are available remedies; a curative petition may be the last judicial resort. A simple executive order cannot overrule a court judgment.
tq: Separate constitutionally recognised remedies from an executive attempt to overrule the judiciary.
sec: Overcoming a judgment - options before government and legislature  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following is the correct distinction between an ordinary validating law and an impermissible legislative overruling of a judgment?
o: The legislature may remove the basis of the judgment by a valid law but cannot merely declare the judgment wrong.
The legislature may nullify any judgment by passing an ordinary resolution.
An ordinary law can breach the Basic Structure if it is passed unanimously.
Only an executive order can remove the basis of a judgment.
x: The legislature may alter the legal basis on which a judgment rests through a valid law, but it cannot simply declare the judicial decision invalid. Neither an amendment nor a law may violate the Basic Structure.
tq: Apply the difference between changing the legal basis and directly overruling the court.
sec: Overcoming a judgment - options before government and legislature  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The constitutional theory underlying judicial review in India is principally the theory of:
o: Supremacy of the Constitution and limited government
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government. India combines elements of American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary supremacy, while Parliament remains subject to the Constitution.
tq: Reject absolute formulations and identify the constitutional limitation underlying review.
sec: Judicial review as a symbol of which government and its theory  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian constitutional system:
1. Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense.
2. Fundamental Rights and federal division limit Parliament’s authority.
3. The power of constitutional amendment is unlimited in India.
4. Judicial review is a feature of the constitutional scheme.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Parliament’s amending power is limited by the Basic Structure doctrine, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Spot the extreme claim of an unlimited power in an otherwise accurate constitutional description.
sec: Basic structure as a limit - supremacy of Constitution, not of courts or Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Supreme Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Constitutional Amendment that excluded judicial review in:
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
x: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to exclude judicial review. Judicial review itself is regarded as part of the Basic Structure.
tq: Use the case-specific holding rather than associating every Basic Structure issue with Kesavananda Bharati.
sec: Basic structure as a limit - supremacy of Constitution, not of courts or Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Which of the following are recognised as elements of the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
1. Judicial review
2. Independence of the judiciary
3. Powers of the Supreme Court under Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142
4. Power of Parliament to destroy Fundamental Rights without limitation

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Judicial review, judicial independence and the specified constitutional powers of the Supreme Court form part of the Basic Structure. Parliament has no unlimited power to destroy Fundamental Rights.
tq: Identify the one proposition that contradicts the limitation imposed by the Basic Structure doctrine.
sec: Basic structure as a limit - supremacy of Constitution, not of courts or Parliament  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
With reference to Article 361 of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. The President and Governors are not answerable to any court for the exercise of their powers and duties.
2. No process for arrest or imprisonment can issue against the President or a Governor during their term of office.
3. A court may issue a writ of mandamus directly against the President or Governor to compel the exercise of a power.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Article 361 protects the President and Governors from being answerable to courts for official acts and bars arrest or imprisonment during their term. A writ of mandamus cannot be issued directly against them, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Separate constitutional personal immunity from the reviewability of government action.
sec: Actions of Governor and President - reviewability  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the 38th and 44th Constitutional Amendments on the satisfaction of the President or Governor?
o: The 38th Amendment made specified satisfactions non-justiciable, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
The 38th Amendment introduced judicial review and the 44th Amendment abolished it.
Both Amendments permanently excluded judicial review of all executive satisfaction.
The 38th Amendment applied only to Governors and the 44th Amendment only to the President.
x: The 38th Amendment (1975) made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable; the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed that position.
tq: Track the before-and-after constitutional change instead of treating the two amendments as identical.
sec: Actions of Governor and President - reviewability  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
sec: Actions of Governor and President - reviewability  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following statements regarding the power of High Courts over laws is correct?
o: A High Court may declare a central law invalid within the scope of its judicial review.
High Courts can review only State laws and never central laws.
High Courts may invalidate constitutional amendments on any policy ground.
The 42nd Amendment permanently prohibited High Courts from reviewing central laws.
x: High Courts can declare central laws invalid in appropriate proceedings. The 42nd Amendment’s bar was removed by the 43rd Amendment, while constitutional amendments can be challenged only on Basic Structure grounds, not merely policy disagreement.
tq: Avoid the reversed scope trap concerning central laws and constitutional amendments.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts’ power to review central laws was removed by the:
x: The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 removed that restriction.
tq: Use the amendment sequence to identify the restoring constitutional change.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 39th Constitutional Amendment:
1. It placed election disputes concerning the Prime Minister, President, Vice-President and Speaker beyond judicial scrutiny.
2. The relevant provision was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain.
3. It was upheld because Parliament’s amending power is unlimited.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The 39th Amendment attempted to place specified election disputes beyond the courts, and the relevant clause was struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975). Statement 3 is false because Parliament’s amending power is limited by the Basic Structure doctrine.
tq: Find the legally significant consequence while rejecting the absolute claim about Parliament’s power.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the constitutional position of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule?
o: Every Ninth Schedule law enjoys blanket immunity from judicial review.
Only laws added before 24 April 1973 can be reviewed for violation of Fundamental Rights.
Laws added after 24 April 1973 may be reviewed if they damage the Basic Structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Ninth Schedule laws are governed exclusively by Article 32 and not by the Basic Structure doctrine.
x: I.R. Coelho (2007) held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to review if they damage the Basic Structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21. The Ninth Schedule therefore provides no blanket immunity.
tq: Look for the date-based qualification that defeats an absolute immunity claim.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Article 31B, which provides constitutional protection to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, was introduced by the:
x: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule were introduced by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951. The protection is not absolute after the ruling in I.R. Coelho.
tq: Match the constitutional provision with the amendment that originally introduced it.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The Ninth Schedule presently contains approximately:
o: More than 180 entries but fewer than 200
x: The Ninth Schedule contains over 280 entries. Its size does not confer blanket immunity from judicial review.
tq: Select the stated range rather than assuming that the Schedule has a fixed constitutional number of entries.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. First Constitutional Amendment introducing Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule
B. Kesavananda Bharati judgment
C. Waman Rao judgment
D. I.R. Coelho judgment

Select the correct sequence.
x: The First Amendment was enacted in 1951, Kesavananda Bharati was decided in 1973, Waman Rao in 1981, and I.R. Coelho in 2007.
tq: Fix the earliest amendment and latest case first, then place the two Basic Structure decisions between them.
sec: Scope - HC power over central laws, amendments, Ninth Schedule  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The power of a constitutional court to examine laws and executive orders and declare them ultra vires or void is known as
x: Judicial review is the power of courts to test the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions and invalidate those that are ultra vires.
tq: Distinguish the formal power of constitutional scrutiny from activism and restraint.
sec: Meaning and origin - countries, source

s: The doctrine of judicial review was formally established in the United States through which case?
o: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
x: Marbury v. Madison (1803), decided under Chief Justice John Marshall, is regarded as the landmark case establishing judicial review in the United States.
tq: Use the landmark-case and year combination to identify the doctrine’s formal origin.
sec: Meaning and origin - countries, source

s: Who was the Chief Justice of the United States associated with the establishment of judicial review in Marbury v. Madison?
x: Chief Justice John Marshall delivered the significant judgment in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.
tq: Separate the case name from the judge associated with its constitutional principle.
sec: Meaning and origin - countries, source

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review exists in countries having written constitutions such as Canada and Australia.
2. The United Kingdom permits judicial review of Acts of Parliament in the same manner as the United States.
3. Parliamentary sovereignty is a characteristic of the British constitutional system.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Judicial review exists in countries such as Canada and Australia. The United Kingdom does not permit courts to invalidate Acts of Parliament in the same manner because of parliamentary sovereignty.
tq: Find the reversed comparison between written-constitution systems and British parliamentary sovereignty.
sec: Meaning and origin - countries, source

s: Sir Edward Coke’s resistance to King James I in seventeenth-century England is regarded as an early root of
x: Sir Edward Coke’s resistance to King James I is cited as an early historical root of the idea that judicial authority can control the exercise of governmental power.
tq: Link the historical personality and event with the constitutional principle they represent.
sec: Meaning and origin - countries, source

s:
With reference to judicial review in India and the United States, consider the following statements:
1. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution uses the expression ‘procedure established by law’.
2. The United States Constitution is associated with the expression ‘due process of law’.
3. The Indian scope of judicial review is generally narrower than the United States scope in this respect.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Indian review under ‘procedure established by law’ traditionally focuses on legal validity and procedure, while American due process includes procedural and substantive fairness.
tq: Compare the exact constitutional phrases before judging the broader legal consequence.
sec: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

s: The description of the United States Supreme Court as a ‘third chamber’ primarily indicates its extensive role in
o: Reviewing and shaping governmental policy through constitutional adjudication
x: The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
tq: Interpret the institutional metaphor rather than treating it as a literal constitutional body.
sec: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

s: Which one of the following best describes the approach of courts towards political and policy questions?
o: Courts ordinarily avoid deciding matters that are purely political or policy-oriented.
Courts can replace every legislative policy with their preferred policy.
Courts must decide every policy question whenever a writ petition is filed.
Courts cannot examine any executive decision involving policy.
x: Courts generally exercise restraint in purely political and policy matters, while retaining the power to examine unconstitutional or capricious action.
tq: Distinguish judicial restraint from the extreme claim that policy matters are entirely immune from review.
sec: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

s: With reference to delimitation decisions, which one of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Courts may undertake limited review where the delimitation decision is capricious.
Delimitation is completely beyond judicial scrutiny in every circumstance.
Every delimitation order must be reconsidered by the Supreme Court on merits.
Delimitation is decided exclusively by the President without statutory authority.
x: Judicial review of delimitation is limited, but it may be possible where the decision is capricious. The principle was noted in Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod (2024).
tq: Watch for the absolute word ‘completely’ and apply the limited-review exception.
sec: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

s: A writ petition is generally refused by a constitutional court when
o: an effective alternative remedy is available
the respondent is a public authority
the petitioner raises a constitutional question
x: Writ jurisdiction is discretionary. Courts may refuse to exercise it where an effective alternative remedy is available, subject to recognised exceptions.
tq: Identify the procedural limitation that makes writ jurisdiction discretionary rather than automatic.
sec: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

s:
Arrange the following stages in the development of judicial activism in India in chronological order:
A. Recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy
B. Expansion of Article 21 through livelihood, education, health and environmental rights
C. Emergence of activism after the Emergency
D. Governance and accountability cases involving matters such as 2G and coal blocks
x: The sequence is: post-Emergency activism in the mid-1970s, expansion of Article 21 from 1979 to the 1980s, governance cases from the 1990s onward, and Puttaswamy in 2017.
tq: Fix the landmark year of Puttaswamy first and then arrange the earlier stages.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mid-1970s — Post-Emergency emergence of judicial activism
2017 — First recognition of speedy trial in Hussainara Khatoon
x: Judicial activism emerged as a new feature of the Indian judiciary in the post-Emergency period, especially through the work associated with Justices Krishna Iyer and Bhagwati.
tq: Match the stage with its defining feature and reject unrelated constitutional events.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: The opening of access to courts through the efforts associated with Justices V. R. Krishna Iyer and P. N. Bhagwati occurred principally during the
x: The post-Emergency period in the mid-1970s marked the emergence of judicial activism and wider access to justice associated with these judges.
tq: Use the period-based chronology rather than confusing it with the later PIL cases.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the expansion of Article 21 during the 1979–1980s stage of judicial activism?
o: Constitutional recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy
x: Privacy was recognised as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy in 2017. The earlier stage involved expansion of Article 21 to livelihood, education, health and a clean environment.
tq: Separate the 1979–1980s Article 21 developments from the later 2017 privacy ruling.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: From the 1990s onward, judicial activism in India increasingly focused on
o: Exclusive adjudication of private contractual disputes
Replacement of written law by customary law
x: The later stage included governance and accountability interventions such as the CVC case, 2G case, coal block cancellation, the Jharkhand Assembly case and directions concerning candidates’ affidavits.
tq: Identify the broad theme that unifies the listed governance cases.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: Which one of the following developments is associated with the year 2017 in the evolution of judicial activism in India?
o: Workplace sexual harassment guidelines in Vishaka
Police reform directions in Prakash Singh
Recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy
x: In 2017, the Supreme Court in Puttaswamy recognised privacy as a fundamental right.
tq: Use the year-case association to distinguish later activism from earlier PIL cases.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial dynamism is another expression used for judicial activism.
2. Judicial activism is generally regarded as the antithesis of judicial restraint.
3. Judicial activism and judicial restraint necessarily require identical judicial approaches.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Judicial dynamism is another term for judicial activism, and activism is contrasted with judicial restraint. The two approaches do not require identical judicial methods.
tq: Reject the absolute equivalence between two contrasting judicial approaches.
sec: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

s: Which one of the following is NOT an evolution genuinely attributed to the Supreme Court?
o: Exemptions to Fundamental Rights expressly written in Articles 31A to 31C and Article 33
x: Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
tq: Distinguish a court-created doctrine from provisions expressly embedded in the Constitution.
sec: Doctrines and remedies evolved by the Supreme Court - genuine vs others

s: The Basic Structure doctrine was evolved by the Supreme Court in
x: The Basic Structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973.
tq: Link the doctrine to its landmark case and year rather than to a later activism remedy.
sec: Doctrines and remedies evolved by the Supreme Court - genuine vs others

s: The judicial direction removing handcuffs from prisoners primarily reflects the expansion of
x: Removal of unnecessary handcuffing is associated with protection of prisoners’ dignity and the broader human-rights dimension of judicial activism.
tq: Identify the constitutional value protected by the remedy instead of the physical measure itself.
sec: Doctrines and remedies evolved by the Supreme Court - genuine vs others

s: When a court keeps a case pending and repeatedly monitors compliance with its directions, the process is called
x: Continuing mandamus keeps the matter open so that the court can monitor implementation and compliance over time.
tq: Match the procedural instrument with its distinctive monitoring function.
sec: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

s: Suo motu cognisance means that
o: the court acts on its own initiative
a private party is compelled to file an appeal
the executive withdraws a pending case
the legislature refers a bill to the court
x: Suo motu cognisance means that the court initiates consideration of a matter on its own motion. It is advised particularly in exceptional cases of constitutional importance.
tq: Use the literal procedural meaning to distinguish suo motu action from party-initiated litigation.
sec: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued by the Supreme Court primarily to
o: fill a legislative vacuum relating to workplace sexual harassment
abolish the writ jurisdiction of High Courts
x: The Vishaka Guidelines of 1997 addressed workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation and operated until the POSH Act, 2013.
tq: Identify the subject of the guidelines and distinguish them from other activism cases.
sec: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

s: Article 142 of the Constitution is relevant to judicial activism because it enables the Supreme Court to
o: make laws for every subject in the Union List
remove elected State governments without constitutional procedure
do complete justice and provide interim remedies where legislative delay creates difficulty
x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, including interim remedies in situations involving legislative delay and institutional deadlock.
tq: Identify the constitutional power from its precise function rather than from an exaggerated legislative claim.
sec: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

s: Court-appointed expert committees are primarily used to
o: provide information and monitor compliance with judicial directions
x: Expert committees assist courts by supplying technical information and helping monitor the implementation of directions.
tq: Match the institutional instrument with its supporting and monitoring role.
sec: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Hussainara Khatoon — Speedy trial for undertrials and first PIL
Olga Tellis — Workplace sexual harassment guidelines
Prakash Singh — Right to livelihood of pavement dwellers
x: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) is associated with speedy trial for undertrials and is regarded as the first PIL. Olga Tellis concerned livelihood, Vishaka workplace harassment and Prakash Singh police reforms.
tq: Start with the sure case-outcome pair and eliminate swapped judicial remedies.
sec: Activism cases

s: The decision in Olga Tellis is primarily associated with the proposition that
o: workplace harassment guidelines are constitutionally mandatory
the right to livelihood is included within Article 21
police officers must have fixed tenure
x: Olga Tellis (1985) recognised the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers as part of the protection afforded by Article 21.
tq: Match the case with its specific Article 21 expansion.
sec: Activism cases

s: The M. C. Mehta cases are significant for
o: wide-ranging environmental directions, although some directions were criticised as policy-making
creating the first State Security Commission
x: The M. C. Mehta cases from the 1980s onward produced extensive environmental directions and also generated debate about judicial policy-making.
tq: Retain both the substantive outcome and the criticism attached to the case group.
sec: Activism cases

s: The Vishaka judgment was delivered in
x: The Vishaka judgment was delivered in 1997 and laid down guidelines concerning sexual harassment at the workplace before the POSH Act, 2013.
tq: Use the four case-year alternatives to identify the chronology of activism cases.
sec: Activism cases

s: The directions in Prakash Singh are associated with
o: The right to livelihood of pavement dwellers
Police reforms, including State Security Commissions and fixed tenure
x: Prakash Singh (2006) concerned police reforms, including directions relating to State Security Commissions and fixed tenure for police personnel.
tq: Identify the institutional reform linked to the case rather than a rights-based Article 21 case.
sec: Activism cases

s:
Which of the following are recognised significance and criticisms of judicial activism?
1. It democratises access to justice.
2. It can force executive accountability.
3. It may blur the separation of powers.
4. It has no effect on the workload of courts.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Judicial activism has democratised access to justice and promoted executive accountability, but it can also blur separation of powers and contribute to overburdened courts. Statement 4 is incorrect.
tq: Accept the two positive functions and reject the absolute claim that activism has no workload consequences.
sec: Universal angles

s: As of May 2022, approximately what proportion of the more than 4.7 crore pending cases was reported to be in subordinate courts?
x: More than 4.7 crore cases were pending, with approximately 87% reported to be in subordinate courts.
tq: Use the magnitude and percentage together to identify the correct pendency figure.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Arrange the following locations of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in chronological order:
A. Amaravati
B. Hyderabad
C. Guntur
D. Common High Court after the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation
x: The High Court moved from Guntur in 1954 to Hyderabad in 1956, became part of the common High Court arrangement in 2014, and shifted to Amaravati in 2019.
tq: Fix the first and last locations, then place Hyderabad and the common High Court in between.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the significance of fast-track courts in the judicial-debate context?
o: They may add speed without adding judges, leaving structural capacity concerns unresolved.
They necessarily reduce pendency by appointing more judges.
They transfer all constitutional cases to the executive.
They eliminate the need for subordinate courts.
x: A criticism of fast-track courts is that they may increase the speed of disposal without increasing the number of judges, thereby not fully addressing structural capacity problems.
tq: Distinguish procedural acceleration from an increase in judicial capacity.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following recent developments is correctly matched?
o: Lisa Gill — first woman Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court, recommended in February 2026
Pakistan’s 27th Amendment — creation of the Ninth Schedule in India
First Amendment of India — establishment of Pakistan’s Federal Constitutional Court
x: Lisa Gill was recommended as the first woman Chief Justice of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in February 2026. The other pairs incorrectly interchange unrelated developments.
tq: Match the person and current institutional development while rejecting cross-country and cross-case swaps.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Supreme Court’s decision to shift contempt pleas concerning ‘bulldozer justice’ to High Courts was principally justified on the ground that High Courts
o: are better placed for fact inquiry
have exclusive authority over contempt of the Supreme Court
x: The shift was linked to the view that High Courts are better placed to undertake fact-finding in such matters.
tq: Identify the practical institutional reason for transferring a matter to a lower constitutional court.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following developments reflects the debate over federal consultation in judicial appointments?
o: The Centre transferred all State judges to subordinate courts without consultation.
The Parliament removed the collegium through an ordinary executive order.
The Supreme Court abolished all High Courts in the States.
The Punjab Cabinet objected that the Centre bypassed State consultation in appointing a High Court Chief Justice.
x: The Punjab Cabinet objected that the Centre had bypassed consultation with the State in relation to the appointment of a High Court Chief Justice.
tq: Identify the federal-consultation issue instead of accepting exaggerated claims about abolition or transfer.
sec: Universal angles

s: The First Constitutional Amendment, whose seventy-fifth anniversary was noted in 2026, received presidential assent on
x: The First Constitutional Amendment received assent on 18 June 1951 and created the Ninth Schedule.
